data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["A base-rate classifier is a statistical null; a placebo checklist is a procedural null.","Base-rate artifacts are properties of the task distribution; placebo effects are properties of the judge's psychology.","Base-rate artifacts are more likely under skew; placebo effects are more likely under high face-validity."],"overturn_conditions":["If the panel's accuracy is high even after subtracting the base-rate benchmark's accuracy, the artifact explanation fails.","If the expert also merely predicts the base rate, the comparison is moot."],"shared_structure":["Both explanations invoke a null model (placebo / base-rate) that can achieve apparent success without genuine task-discrimination.","Both require comparing the treatment (checklist / panel) against the null model on the same outcome metric.","Both reveal that high apparent performance can be uninformative about the underlying mechanism."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_006","SCR_001"],"transfer_claims":["The concept of 'incremental validity over a null model' transfers: a panel must beat the base-rate classifier to claim genuine discrimination.","The warning against accuracy as a metric under class imbalance transfers: high accuracy can mask zero discrimination.","The need for a pre-registered benchmark transfers: if the base-rate benchmark is computed post-hoc, it can be cherry-picked to make the panel look good."]},"claim":"The non-expert panel's apparent superiority is often a baseline-rate artifact: when outcomes are highly skewed, a checklist with high inter-rater agreement will appear highly reliable while merely encoding the base rate, making it statistically indistinguishable from a trivial classifier. Within a single evaluation, one can detect this by comparing the panel's accuracy to the base-rate classifier's accuracy on the same case-set; if the incremental accuracy is negligible, the gain is mere compliance, not genuine discrimination.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the task is balanced (base rate near 50%), the base-rate artifact vanishes and high accuracy cannot be explained by mere compliance.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the expert is also subject to base-rate neglect, the panel may genuinely win by encoding the base rate, but this is a calibration gain, not a discrimination gain.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the evaluation uses a proper scoring rule (e.g., Brier score) that penalizes base-rate-following, the artifact is mitigated and the test is less necessary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"In highly skewed domains (e.g., rare disease screening), a checklist that prompts for common features will lead panelists to the majority-class answer with high agreement. This yields high accuracy and high inter-rater reliability, but the checklist is merely a base-rate heuristic. An expert relying on intuition, even if imperfect, may detect minority-class cues. The panel's 'gain' is an artifact of accuracy being a bad metric under skew. The distinguishing evidence is the panel's incremental validity over the base-rate benchmark on the same cases.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
